implementation_notes: Squants is the library answer: a Quantity is a combination of a numeric value and a UnitOfMeasure, every Dimension (Length, Mass, Time, Velocity, ...) has one primary unit plus unit objects with conversion factors, and the quantity classes define cross-dimensional operators themselves - Length * Length is an Area and Length / Time is a Velocity via the TimeIntegral traits - so derived quantities are typed rather than computed as bare numbers. Values are constructed by applying a unit object to a number (Kilometers(3)), converted with toMeters/toFeet, and all types are immutable and thread-safe. Scala 3 opaque types allow the same guarantee without the library for a project's own small dimension set.
code_sketch:
import squants.space.{Kilometers, Meters, Feet}
import squants.time.Seconds

val span  = Kilometers(3)
val gap   = Meters(500)
val total = span + gap            // 3500.0 m: addition converts
total.toFeet                      // 11482.94 ft
val v = total / Seconds(2)        // 1750.0 m/s, a Velocity
// Kilometers(3) + Seconds(2) does not compile
pitfalls: Unit objects are the API surface, so imports decide meaning: a locally defined Meters next to squants.space.Meters produces confusing type errors or the wrong factor.
Arithmetic works on Double values, so mathematically equal quantities can compare unequal after different conversion paths; compare with an explicit tolerance when that matters.
The implicit DSL (3.kilometers, 1.hour) hides which unit is in play at the call site - keep explicit unit objects in domain code and reserve the DSL for literals.

variants.name: Scala 3 opaque types per unit
variants.idiom_name: opaque type Meters = Double + extension methods
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3 opaque type aliases give type abstraction with no runtime overhead (the representation is erased), which is exactly what a unit wrapper needs: opaque type Meters = Double inside an object, with apply/toFeet extension methods and the conversion factors defined in that scope, so outside the object Meters and Feet are unrelated abstract types and mixing them is a compile error. It is the same idea as a value class but without boxing, and it keeps the dimension algebra hand-rolled - a derived unit must be declared as its own opaque type or computed through a method that names its result type.
variants.code_sketch:
object units:
  opaque type Metres = Double
  opaque type Feet = Double

  object Metres:
    def apply(d: Double): Metres = d
  object Feet:
    def apply(d: Double): Feet = d
  extension (m: Metres)
    def toFeet: Feet = Feet(m / 0.3048)
    def +(other: Metres): Metres = m + other

import units.*
val total = Metres(3000) + Metres(500)   // Metres(3500.0)
// Metres(3) + Feet(2) does not compile
pitfalls: Within the defining scope the opaque type is transparent, so a stray Double operation inside the companion silently bypasses the abstraction - keep the scope small.
Extension methods are the only public surface; forgetting one (for example a conversion back to Double) pushes users to unsafe casts.
There is no dimensional algebra: multiplication of two opaque quantities needs an explicit declared result type, so compound units stay hand-rolled.
